grade.first_issue: Rule E applies in the finiteness argument: the opening formula requires inclusion-minimal hitting sets, but stabilization of h_n controls only minimum-cardinality hitting sets. An inclusion-minimal hitting set can have more than |Q_1| elements, so S\{p} need not belong to the asserted finite family H_N. Consequently, finiteness of P_global is not established.
grade.summary: The hitting-set reformulation and uniform gap bound are valid, but the central finiteness claim is unsupported. Even conditionally, the finite-state description incorrectly treats every Q_i as a subset of P_global. Finally, the passage from eventual to pure translational periodicity uses an unjustified multiplier and an invalid downward induction. The correct conclusion is therefore not proved.
strengths: Correctly translates the gcd requirement into a hitting-set condition, provided “minimal” means inclusion-minimal.
Correctly observes that Q_1 hits every Q_i and obtains the uniform bound a_{n+1}-a_n <= rad(a_1).
Once a genuinely finite relevant prime universe is available, the proposed finite-state idea is a plausible route to eventual translational periodicity.

errors.description: The proof conflates inclusion-minimal and minimum-cardinality hitting sets. If “minimal” means minimum-cardinality, the initial formula for a_{n+1} is unjustified; if it means inclusion-minimal, the bound |S| <= |Q_1| used in the finiteness argument is false in general.

Finiteness of primes appearing in minimal hitting sets would not imply that each full support Q_i is contained in P_global; sequence terms may have additional prime factors. One would need to replace Q_i by appropriate traces and prove that these traces determine the transition.

The claimed choice of m with mL' divisible by rad(a_1...a_{N+mT'}) is neither proved nor generally available. Moreover, the stated downward-induction hypothesis gives the relation only for indices at least n+1, yet the proof immediately uses it at n-1. Thus the extension from an eventual period to all n fails.
